stem: Your coding agent's main context fills with raw search results and file dumps while it investigates a large codebase. Per Anthropic's context engineering post, how do sub-agent architectures help?

choices.text: Sub-agents share the lead's context, so each search result is cached once
choices.reason: Sub-agents work with clean context windows; the detailed search context stays isolated inside them.

choices.text: Sub-agents remove the need to summarize, by passing back full transcripts
choices.reason: The opposite: each sub-agent returns a condensed, distilled summary, not its full exploration.

choices.text: Sub-agents raise the lead agent's context window limit for that task
choices.reason: They don't enlarge any window; they move focused work into separate, clean windows.

choices.text: Sub-agents explore in clean windows and return only condensed summaries
choices.reason: Correct: a sub-agent may use tens of thousands of tokens but returns a distilled summary, often 1,000-2,000 tokens.

takeaway: Sub-agents keep **detailed search context isolated** and hand the lead agent a condensed summary of their work.
explanation: Sub-agents protect the lead's context by doing focused exploration in **clean, separate windows** and returning only a **condensed, distilled summary**; a sub-agent may use tens of thousands of tokens but hand back often 1,000-2,000 (Option D). Option B is the tempting reversal, since full transcripts would dump the raw results right back into the main context. Option A is wrong because sub-agents don't share the lead's context, and C is wrong because they don't enlarge any window; they move the work elsewhere.

source.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents

stem: In Claude Code you're planning, implementing and testing one feature, with constant back-and-forth as requirements shift. A teammate suggests sending each phase to its own subagent. What do the Claude Code docs recommend?

choices.text: Use a subagent per phase so that each phase starts with a clean context window
choices.reason: A subagent that isn't a fork starts fresh and may need time to gather context; phases that share context would lose it.

choices.text: Keep it in the main conversation; the phases share significant context
choices.reason: Correct: use the main conversation for frequent back-and-forth and when phases like planning, implementation and testing share context.

choices.text: Use a Skill instead, because Skills run in an isolated subagent context
choices.reason: Skills run in the main conversation context; the docs suggest them for reusable prompts or workflows, not isolation.

choices.text: Use subagents so the phases finish faster than in the main conversation
choices.reason: The docs list latency as a reason to stay in the main conversation: a non-fork subagent starts fresh and may need time.

takeaway: Subagents suit **self-contained work that returns a summary**; iterative, context-sharing work belongs in the main conversation.
explanation: The docs say subagents suit **self-contained** work that returns a summary, while frequent back-and-forth and phases that **share significant context** belong in the main conversation (Option B). The stem's clues are shifting requirements and planning, implementing and testing the same feature. Option A is the tempting trap: a clean window sounds good, but a non-fork subagent starts fresh and would lose the shared context. Option D gets latency backwards for the same reason, and C is wrong because Skills run in the main conversation context.

stem: You're evaluating Strands Agents for a support bot. A teammate asks what the SDK's foundational concept is and how it decides a task is finished. Which description matches the Strands docs?

choices.text: A model-driven loop: call the model, run requested tools, repeat until it answers
choices.reason: Correct: the loop invokes the model, executes requested tools, feeds results back, and repeats until the model produces a final response.

choices.text: A fixed graph of nodes your code defines in advance and then runs in strict order
choices.reason: That describes a predefined workflow; in the Strands loop the model decides at each step whether to act or respond.

choices.text: A planner that writes the whole tool sequence up front, then executes it exactly once
choices.reason: The model decides autonomously at each iteration based on its evolving understanding, not from one fixed plan.

choices.text: A router that classifies each request and returns one tool's raw output
choices.reason: The loop continues across many tool calls, feeding each result back to the model until it responds.

takeaway: Strands is built on a **model-driven agent loop**: reason, select a tool, run it, feed the result back, until a final response.
explanation: Strands is built on a **model-driven agent loop**: invoke the model, execute any tools it requests, feed the results back, and repeat until the model produces a final response (Option A). The key idea is that the model decides at each step whether to act or answer. Option C is the tempting trap because it sounds agentic, but it fixes the whole plan up front instead of deciding per iteration. Option B describes a predefined workflow, and D stops after one tool's raw output rather than looping.

diagram.caption: The Strands agent loop repeats until the model responds without a tool call.

stem: In your Strands agent, a database tool sometimes throws a timeout. You want to know what the agent loop does when a tool fails during execution. Which behavior do the Strands docs describe?

choices.text: The loop raises the exception and ends the invocation immediately
choices.reason: Failures go back as error results 'rather than throwing an exception that terminates the loop'.

choices.text: The loop silently drops the tool call and continues as if it succeeded
choices.reason: The execution system captures failures and sends the error information to the model; nothing is dropped silently.

choices.text: The error goes back to the model as an error result so it can recover
choices.reason: Correct: a failure returns to the model as an error result, giving it an opportunity to recover or try alternatives.

choices.text: The loop pauses and waits for a human to approve another attempt
choices.reason: Pausing for human input is what interrupts are for; a failed tool simply becomes an error result for the model.

takeaway: In the Strands loop a failing tool becomes an **error result** for the model, not a crash, so the agent can recover.
explanation: In the Strands loop, the execution system captures a tool failure and sends it back to the model as an **error result**, rather than throwing an exception that terminates the loop, so the model can recover or try alternatives (Option C). Option A is the tempting assumption from ordinary code, where an uncaught exception ends execution. Option B is wrong because nothing is dropped silently; the error information reaches the model. Option D confuses failures with interrupts, which are the mechanism for pausing for human input.

stem: Your Strands agent makes many tool calls on long tasks and starts failing with input-length errors from the model provider. Which fixes do the Strands docs suggest for context window exhaustion?

choices.text: Make tools return summaries or relevant excerpts instead of full data
choices.reason: Correct: reducing tool output verbosity is a listed fix, since every loop iteration adds results to the history.

choices.text: Nest tool schemas more deeply so parameters are better organized
choices.reason: The docs advise simplifying schemas: deeply nested schemas consume tokens in the tool config and the model's reasoning.

choices.text: Disable the conversation manager so earlier messages are never altered or dropped
choices.reason: The docs suggest configuring a conversation manager (sliding window by default, or summarization) to keep history in bounds.

choices.text: Decompose large tasks into subtasks, each handled with a fresh context
choices.reason: Correct: splitting the work so each subtask gets a fresh context is one of the listed solutions.

choices.text: Keep every past tool result so the model never loses earlier details
choices.reason: Accumulating every result is what exhausts the window; the docs suggest trimming output and managing history.

takeaway: Context fills because **every loop iteration adds history**: trim tool output, manage the conversation, and split big tasks.
explanation: Every loop iteration **adds results to the history**, so long tool-heavy runs exhaust the window. The listed fixes include making tools return **summaries or relevant excerpts** (A) and **decomposing large tasks** so each subtask gets a fresh context (D). Option E is the most tempting wrong pick since keeping details sounds safe, but accumulating every result is the cause. Option C disables the conversation manager the docs suggest configuring, and B goes the wrong way, since deeply nested schemas consume tokens.

stem: In your incident tool, a monitoring agent detects an issue and hands off to a network specialist, who may hand off to a database admin. The path emerges from each agent's findings. Which Strands multi-agent pattern fits?

choices.text: Workflow: a fixed task graph (DAG) your code defines and runs as one tool
choices.reason: A Workflow fixes the path in a dependency graph and allows no cycles; here the path emerges from the agents.

choices.text: Graph: a developer-defined flowchart with every node and edge set in advance
choices.reason: A Graph suits structured processes with conditional branching; its path still follows the edges you define.

choices.text: Agents as tools: one orchestrator calls each specialist and stays in charge
choices.reason: That keeps one orchestrator delegating; here each agent itself hands control to the most suitable peer.

choices.text: Swarm: a pool of specialized agents that hand off tasks to each other
choices.reason: Correct: the Strands docs use multidisciplinary incident response as a Swarm example; the agents decide the path.

takeaway: Strands: **Workflow** = fixed DAG, **Graph** = defined flowchart with LLM-chosen branches, **Swarm** = emergent handoffs between agents.
explanation: The deciding detail is that the handoff path **emerges from each agent's findings**, with each agent passing control to a suitable peer. That is a **Swarm**, and the Strands docs use multidisciplinary incident response as its example (Option D). Option B is the tempting look-alike, since a Graph supports conditional branching, but its path still follows edges you define. A Workflow (A) fixes the path in a DAG with no cycles, and agents as tools (C) keeps one orchestrator in charge.

stem: Your Strands app has a general orchestrator agent and a weather specialist agent. You want the orchestrator to call the specialist only when a query is about weather. What is the simplest way, per the Strands docs?

choices.text: Build a Graph with an edge from the orchestrator node to the weather node
choices.reason: Graph is for structured orchestration with branches and loops; the docs call agents as tools the simplest composition.

choices.text: Pass the specialist agent directly in the orchestrator's tools list
choices.reason: Correct: the orchestrator reads the specialist's description and calls it when the query fits, like any other tool.

choices.text: Run both agents on every query and merge their answers afterward
choices.reason: Running both every time isn't calling the specialist only when it fits; the orchestrator should decide.

choices.text: Connect them over the Agent-to-Agent protocol as separate services
choices.reason: A2A connects agents running as separate services; two agents in one app can simply be composed as tools.

takeaway: In Strands the simplest multi-agent setup is **agents as tools**: pass a specialist agent in an orchestrator's tools.
explanation: The simplest composition in Strands is **agents as tools**: pass the specialist agent in the orchestrator's tools list, and the orchestrator reads its description and calls it only when a query fits, like any tool (Option B). Option A is the tempting trap because it works, but Graph is meant for structured orchestration with branches and loops, which is more than needed here. Option C calls the specialist on every query, ignoring the "only when" requirement, and D's A2A protocol is for agents running as separate services.

stem: Your team is building a ticket classifier: one model from one provider, two tools, a single agent, short bounded runs, and a runtime where every dependency is a real cost. Per Strands' own guide to choosing an agent foundation, what should it run on?

choices.text: A hand-written loop, since a framework's features would go unused
choices.reason: Correct: the guide says a hand-written loop is the better call when most of these hold: one provider, few tools, short runs, minimal dependencies.

choices.text: A framework, because a hand-written loop can't call tools reliably
choices.reason: The guide says almost every agent starts as a while loop that calls the model and tools, and that's the right way to begin.

choices.text: A multi-agent framework, so routing is ready if a second agent arrives
choices.reason: With a single agent, multi-agent orchestration has nothing to orchestrate; the guide says add jobs as you need them.

choices.text: A hosted agent platform, since Strands needs its own control plane
choices.reason: Strands runs in your own process as a library, with no hosted control plane; and this agent may not need a framework at all.

takeaway: A small, single-provider, short-run agent is fine on a **hand-written loop**; adopt a framework when you need several of its jobs at once.
explanation: Strands' guide says a **hand-written loop** is the better call when most of these hold: one provider, few tools, short runs, minimal dependencies. The stem ticks every box, including dependencies being a real cost, so a framework's features would go unused (Option A). Option C is the tempting future-proofing move, but with a single agent there is nothing to orchestrate; add jobs as you need them. Option B is false since almost every agent starts as a while loop, and D is wrong because Strands runs in your process with no hosted control plane.

stem: You're reviewing a LangGraph project for the first time. The code defines a `StateGraph`, calls `add_node` and `add_edge`, then compiles it. How do LangGraph's docs describe the roles of its three core components?

choices.text: Nodes store the shared data, edges call the LLM, and state routes the flow
choices.reason: Reversed: state is the shared snapshot, nodes do the work, and edges decide what runs next.

choices.text: State is the prompt, nodes are tools, and edges are the model's tool calls
choices.reason: Nodes and edges are just functions that can contain an LLM or plain code; state is a shared data structure.

choices.text: State is a shared snapshot, nodes do the work, and edges pick what runs next
choices.reason: Correct: state is the shared snapshot, nodes encode logic and return updates, and edges choose the next node. Nodes do the work, edges tell what to do next.

choices.text: State is optional, nodes must call an LLM, and edges allow only straight paths
choices.reason: Edges can be conditional branches or fixed transitions, and nodes can contain an LLM or just ordinary code.

takeaway: LangGraph = **state** (shared snapshot) + **nodes** (do the work) + **edges** (decide what runs next).
explanation: LangGraph has three roles: **state** is the shared snapshot, **nodes** encode logic and return updates (they do the work), and **edges** choose which node runs next (Option C). Option A is the tempting trap because it uses the right words with the roles scrambled. Option B narrows nodes to tools and edges to tool calls, when both are just functions that can contain an LLM or plain code. Option D is wrong on all counts: nodes need not call an LLM, and edges can be conditional branches as well as fixed transitions.

stem: Your LangGraph agent must pause before issuing a refund, wait for a manager's approval, then continue. You'll call `interrupt()` inside the approval node. What else do LangGraph's docs say you need?

choices.text: A second graph that polls for the approval and restarts the first one
choices.reason: You resume by re-invoking the same graph with a Command; its value becomes interrupt()'s return value.

choices.text: A checkpointer to persist the graph state while it is paused
choices.reason: Correct: interrupt() saves the graph state through the persistence layer; use a durable checkpointer in production.

choices.text: A static breakpoint set on every node so the pause can happen anywhere in the graph
choices.reason: Interrupts are dynamic: they can be placed anywhere in node code and be conditional, unlike static breakpoints.

choices.text: A thread ID in the config so the runtime knows which state to resume
choices.reason: Correct: thread_id is the pointer that tells the checkpointer which saved state to load when you resume.

choices.text: A payload of Python objects that need not be JSON-serializable
choices.reason: The docs say the value passed to interrupt() must be JSON-serializable.

takeaway: LangGraph **interrupts** need a checkpointer and a thread_id: the state is saved, then resumed with a `Command`.
explanation: `interrupt()` pauses by saving graph state through the persistence layer, so you need a **checkpointer** to hold the paused state (B), and a **thread ID** in the config that tells the checkpointer which saved state to load when you resume (D). Option C is the most tempting wrong pick, but interrupts are dynamic and can sit anywhere in node code, unlike static breakpoints. Option A is unnecessary since you resume the same graph with a `Command`, and E is wrong because the interrupt value must be JSON-serializable.

stem: Your LangGraph assistant should remember each user's preferred language across all of their separate conversations (threads), not just within one. Which LangGraph persistence feature fits?

choices.text: A checkpointer, since it persists the graph state as checkpoints
choices.reason: Checkpointers persist one thread's graph state: short-term, thread-scoped memory, not data shared across threads.

choices.text: A larger state schema, with the preference stored as a graph key
choices.reason: Graph state is persisted per thread by the checkpointer, so it doesn't reach the user's other threads.

choices.text: An `InMemorySaver` checkpointer, so preferences survive restarts
choices.reason: InMemorySaver keeps checkpoints in RAM and loses them on restart, and checkpointers are thread-scoped anyway.

choices.text: A store, which keeps application data outside the graph state
choices.reason: Correct: stores hold long-term, cross-thread memory such as user preferences, facts and shared knowledge.

takeaway: LangGraph **checkpointers** = short-term, per-thread state; **stores** = long-term memory shared across threads.
explanation: The key word is **across** threads. Checkpointers persist one thread's graph state, which is short-term, thread-scoped memory; a **store** keeps long-term, cross-thread data such as user preferences outside the graph state (Option D). Option A is the tempting trap, since a checkpointer does persist state, just not beyond its thread. Option B stores the preference in graph state, which is still persisted per thread, and C keeps checkpoints in RAM, losing them on restart while still being thread-scoped.

stem: Your PydanticAI agent extracts invoices, and downstream code needs a typed `Invoice` object from every run, not free text it has to parse. What does PydanticAI provide for this?

choices.text: Ask for JSON in the instructions and parse the reply with `json.loads`
choices.reason: That leaves parsing and validation to you; with output_type, PydanticAI builds the schema and validates the data.

choices.text: Register `Invoice` as a function tool the model may call when ready
choices.reason: Function tools are optional calls whose results go back to the model; an output type is what the run must end with.

choices.text: Set the agent's `output_type` to the `Invoice` Pydantic model
choices.reason: Correct: Pydantic builds the JSON schema from the model, validates the returned data, and result.output is typed as Invoice.

choices.text: Post-process every reply with a regex that maps text into `Invoice` fields
choices.reason: That is hand-rolled parsing; with output_type, Pydantic builds the schema and validates the model's data for you.

takeaway: In PydanticAI, set **output_type** to a Pydantic model: the run returns validated, typed data instead of free text.
explanation: Setting the agent's `output_type` to the `Invoice` Pydantic model makes PydanticAI build the JSON schema, validate the returned data, and type `result.output` as `Invoice` (Option C). The stem's need is typed, validated data from **every run**, not text to parse. Option B is the tempting trap, but a function tool is an optional call whose result goes back to the model, while an output type is what the run must end with. Options A and D are hand-rolled parsing that leave validation to you.

stem: Your PydanticAI agent's tools call a payments API through an HTTP client and an API key. In unit tests you want to swap in a fake client without changing the tools. Which PydanticAI feature is built for this?

choices.text: Module-level globals for the client, monkeypatched in every test that needs a fake
choices.reason: PydanticAI's approach is a type-safe dependency system; tools get dependencies via RunContext, not module globals.

choices.text: Dependency injection via `deps_type` and `RunContext`, overridden in tests
choices.reason: Correct: tools read dependencies from ctx.deps, and you can override an agent's dependencies in tests while calling app code.

choices.text: Output validators that intercept each tool call and replace its result
choices.reason: Output validators check the agent's output and can raise ModelRetry; they don't swap a tool's services.

choices.text: A different `output_type` per environment so tests return fixed objects
choices.reason: Swapping the output type doesn't touch the dependency system; tools get their services from ctx.deps, which tests override.

takeaway: PydanticAI passes services to instructions and tools as **typed dependencies** (`RunContext`), which tests can override.
explanation: PydanticAI has a type-safe **dependency injection** system: declare services with `deps_type`, read them in tools from `ctx.deps` via `RunContext`, and override the agent's dependencies in tests (Option B). That swaps the fake client without changing the tools. Option A is the tempting habit from ordinary Python, but monkeypatching module globals isn't PydanticAI's approach. Option C misuses output validators, which check output and can raise `ModelRetry`, and D changes the output type without touching the dependencies.

stem: You implement the client-side handler for Claude's memory tool. A tester sends a `view` command with the path `/memories/../../secrets.env`. What do the memory tool docs require of your handler?

choices.text: Validate every path: resolve it and reject anything outside `/memories`
choices.reason: Correct: validate every path in every command, resolve it to canonical form, and reject traversal sequences such as ../.

choices.text: Nothing: the API blocks paths outside `/memories` before your handler runs
choices.reason: The tool is client-side: Claude only requests operations and your application executes them, so validation is your job.

choices.text: Trust it, since Claude refuses to write sensitive data to memory files
choices.reason: Claude usually refuses to write sensitive data, but that isn't path protection; the docs require validating every path.

choices.text: Strip the leading `/memories` and serve the rest from your app's root
choices.reason: That would expose files outside the memory directory; restrict all memory operations to /memories.

takeaway: The memory tool runs **client-side**, so your handler must **validate every path** and keep every operation inside `/memories`.
explanation: The memory tool is **client-side**: Claude only requests operations and your application executes them, so security is your handler's job. The docs require validating every path in every command, resolving it to canonical form, and rejecting traversal like `../` that escapes `/memories` (Option A). Option B is the tempting assumption that the API filters paths first, but it doesn't. Option C confuses Claude usually refusing to write sensitive data with path protection, and D would expose files outside the memory directory.

stem: Your agent works for hours on a software project that spans many sessions, using the memory tool. Which practices do the memory tool docs recommend for this kind of long-running work?

choices.text: Write memory files ad hoc whenever the agent happens to learn something
choices.reason: For multi-session projects the docs say to set up memory files deliberately instead of writing them ad hoc.

choices.text: Mark a feature complete as soon as its code has been written
choices.reason: Mark a feature complete only after end-to-end verification confirms it works, not when the code is written.

choices.text: Pair memory with compaction so key facts survive summarization
choices.reason: Correct: compaction keeps the active context small, and memory preserves the information that must survive summarization.

choices.text: Skip reading memory at startup and rebuild state by re-exploring the codebase
choices.reason: Each new session should open by reading the memory files, restoring state without re-exploring the code base.

choices.text: Have an initializer session create a progress log and feature checklist
choices.reason: Correct: the first session sets up memory files before substantive work, including a progress log and a feature checklist.

takeaway: For long-running work, an **initializer** sets up progress and feature files, and **memory plus compaction** keeps what must survive.
explanation: For multi-session work, set memory up **deliberately**: an initializer session creates a progress log and feature checklist before substantive work (E), and pairing memory with **compaction** keeps the active context small while memory preserves what must survive summarization (C). Option A is the most tempting wrong pick, since writing notes as you go sounds helpful, but the docs say not to write them ad hoc. Option B marks features done before end-to-end verification, and D skips reading memory at startup and re-explores the code.

stem: Your harness adds context resets because an older model wrapped up tasks early as its context limit approached. On a newer model that behavior is gone. What lesson does Anthropic's Managed Agents post draw?

choices.text: Keep the resets anyway, since harness safeguards never lose their value
choices.reason: Anthropic found the resets had become dead weight on Claude Opus 4.5 once the behavior was gone.

choices.text: Pin the old model for good so the harness assumptions stay correct
choices.reason: The post's answer is interfaces meant to outlast any particular harness, not freezing the model.

choices.text: Harnesses encode assumptions that go stale as models improve, so revisit them
choices.reason: Correct: harnesses encode assumptions about what Claude can't do; the Sonnet 4.5 context-anxiety fix became dead weight on Opus 4.5.

choices.text: Move to a multi-agent design, since single agents can't handle long tasks
choices.reason: The post draws no such conclusion; its lesson is that harness assumptions should be frequently questioned.

takeaway: Harness workarounds **go stale** as models improve; question them regularly and build on interfaces that outlast them.
explanation: Harnesses **encode assumptions** about what Claude can't do, and those go stale as models improve; the context-reset fix for Sonnet 4.5's early wrap-up became dead weight on Opus 4.5 (Option C). Option A is the tempting safety instinct, but the post found the resets had no remaining value once the behavior was gone. Option B freezes the model instead of building on interfaces meant to outlast any particular harness, and D draws a multi-agent conclusion the post never makes.

source.title: Scaling Managed Agents: Decoupling the brain from the hands

stem: Your team moves a coding agent from a hand-written Messages API loop to the Claude Agent SDK, running it in a container you manage. Which responsibility does the team still keep?

choices.text: Writing the loop that executes each tool call and feeds the result back
choices.reason: The SDK gives you the same agent loop that powers Claude Code. Writing the tool loop yourself is the Client SDK path.

choices.text: Operating the process and infrastructure the agent runs in
choices.reason: Correct: the Agent SDK embeds Claude Code's agent in your own application, in a process you operate. Having Anthropic host the agent is the Managed Agents path.

choices.text: Implementing file read, edit and shell tools for the agent to call
choices.reason: Built-in tools that read, write and edit files, run commands and search the web are among the SDK's capabilities.

choices.text: Building context management for when the conversation grows long
choices.reason: The SDK provides the same context management that powers Claude Code, so you don't build it yourself.

takeaway: The Agent SDK hands you the loop, built-in tools and context management, but it runs **in a process you operate**.
explanation: Each wiring path differs in who runs the agent and what comes built in. The detail that decides it is "a container you manage": the Agent SDK is a library inside your own process, so hosting stays with you, while the loop, tools and context management come with it. Choice A is the tempting one, but writing the tool loop yourself is what the team is leaving behind with the Client SDK.

stem: Your Agent SDK agent runs in `default` mode behind a web app. Before any `Bash` command runs, a person must see it in your UI and approve or reject it. Which setup does that?

choices.text: Add `Bash` to `allowedTools` so each command is routed to your approval screen
choices.reason: An allow rule **auto-approves** the call, and the `canUseTool` callback never fires for auto-approved tools, so nobody would see the command.

choices.text: Include `AskUserQuestion` in `tools` so Claude asks the user before each command
choices.reason: Claude decides when to ask clarifying questions and writes them itself; you can't add your own questions to that flow, so it isn't an approval gate.

choices.text: Pass a `canUseTool` callback that shows the command and returns allow or deny
choices.reason: Correct: the callback fires when Claude wants a tool that isn't auto-approved and pauses execution until you return allow or deny; Claude sees a deny message.

choices.text: Switch to `acceptEdits` mode so commands wait for the user's confirmation
choices.reason: A mode like `acceptEdits` approves calls **before** `canUseTool` is consulted, so anything it approves never reaches a person to confirm.

takeaway: A human approval checkpoint in the SDK is a **`canUseTool` callback**; anything auto-approved earlier never reaches it.
explanation: The SDK pauses for a person through `canUseTool`, which receives the tool name and input and waits until you return allow or deny. The stem needs **every** `Bash` command shown to a human, so nothing may auto-approve it first. Choice A is the trap: listing `Bash` in `allowedTools` sounds like registering it for review, but an allow rule approves the call before the callback is ever consulted.

stem: You're replacing your hand-written Messages API loop with the Claude Agent SDK. Which jobs does the SDK now do for you, so you can delete that code?

choices.text: Running each tool Claude requests and collecting the results
choices.reason: Correct: in the SDK's loop, the SDK runs each requested tool and collects the results, which feed back to Claude for the next decision.

choices.text: Choosing which tools may run without anyone having to approve them
choices.reason: Still yours: `allowed_tools`, `disallowed_tools` and `permission_mode` decide what runs automatically and what needs approval.

choices.text: Sending results back and repeating until a reply has no tool calls
choices.reason: Correct: turns continue without yielding control back to your code, until Claude produces output with no tool calls.

choices.text: Capping how many turns or how many dollars a single run is allowed to use
choices.reason: Still yours: `max_turns` and `max_budget_usd` default to no limit, so you set them; a budget is a good default for production agents.

choices.text: Checking whether the run succeeded before reading its final text
choices.reason: Still yours: check the `ResultMessage` `subtype` first, because the `result` field is present only on `success`.

takeaway: The SDK runs the tools and the loop; **permissions, limits and result checks** stay in your code.
explanation: Moving to the SDK removes the loop mechanics: executing each tool and feeding results back until Claude replies without tool calls. The words "do for you" rule out the configuration choices, which the SDK only enforces once you set them. Choice D is the most tempting, but turn and budget limits default to none, so leaving them out means an open-ended prompt can run long.

stem: Your support agent on the Messages API should recall each customer's stated preferences when they come back weeks later in a brand-new conversation. Which memory pattern fits?

choices.text: External storage: the memory tool, mapping `/memories` to a per-customer store
choices.reason: Correct: the memory tool stores and retrieves information across conversations, and your handler maps `/memories` onto real storage such as a per-user directory.

choices.text: In-context memory: keep the preferences in the conversation history you send
choices.reason: A brand-new conversation doesn't carry the old history. The memory tool exists to keep knowledge across conversations without keeping it all in context.

choices.text: Summarized memory: enable compaction so older turns become a short summary
choices.reason: Compaction summarizes older context **within** a conversation as it nears the window limit; it doesn't carry anything into a new one.

choices.text: No persistent memory: each conversation starts fresh, which suits returning users
choices.reason: Starting fresh means nothing carries over. Memory lives entirely in your application, so recall needs a store your handler serves.

takeaway: Facts that must outlive a conversation need **external storage**, such as the memory tool backed by a store you control.
explanation: The deciding phrase is "weeks later in a brand-new conversation": the memory has to survive the end of a session. Only external storage does that, and with the memory tool your handler maps `/memories` to storage you control. Choice C is tempting because compaction also "remembers" a summary, but it only shrinks history inside one conversation.

stem: Developers on your team paste the same 40-line incident-triage checklist into Claude Code several times a week. It's only needed during incidents. What does the skills documentation recommend?

choices.text: Add the checklist to CLAUDE.md so it's loaded into every session automatically
choices.reason: CLAUDE.md loads every session. The docs say to create a skill when a CLAUDE.md section has grown into a procedure, since a skill body costs almost nothing until used.

choices.text: Turn the checklist into a skill whose body loads only when it's used
choices.reason: Correct: create a skill when you keep pasting the same checklist or procedure into chat; its body loads only when it's used.

choices.text: Keep pasting it, since instructions given in chat only cost context when needed
choices.reason: Pasting the same checklist again and again is exactly the signal the docs give for creating a skill.

choices.text: Make it a skill, but put the full checklist in the skill's `description` field
choices.reason: Skill descriptions are always in context so Claude knows what's available, so a checklist written there would be paid for in every session.

takeaway: A procedure you keep pasting belongs in a **skill**: its description is always in context, its body only when used.
explanation: Skills exist for reusable instructions that shouldn't inflate every session. Two details decide it: the checklist is pasted repeatedly, and it's only needed sometimes. Choice A is tempting because CLAUDE.md also avoids re-pasting, but it loads in every session, which is exactly the cost a skill avoids.

diagram.caption: Until the skill is invoked, only its description is in context.

stem: In your main Claude Code session you invoked the `api-conventions` skill, then delegated endpoint work to a custom `api-developer` subagent (not a fork). Its code ignores the conventions. What makes sure the subagent starts with them?

choices.text: Nothing extra: a subagent sees the skills already invoked in the main session
choices.reason: A subagent starts with a fresh context: it doesn't see your conversation history, the skills you've already invoked, or files Claude has read.

choices.text: Invoke `api-conventions` again in the main session just before delegating
choices.reason: That content lands in the main conversation, which the subagent never sees; it works from Claude's delegation message.

choices.text: List `api-conventions` in the subagent's `skills` frontmatter field
choices.reason: Correct: the `skills` field injects the full content of each listed skill into the subagent's context at startup.

choices.text: Rely on the Skill tool, which loads every project skill as a subagent starts
choices.reason: Without the field, the subagent can discover and invoke skills **during** execution through the Skill tool; nothing is preloaded at startup.

takeaway: Subagents don't inherit the skills you invoked; **preload** them with the subagent's `skills` field.
explanation: A non-fork subagent starts from a fresh context window, so whatever was invoked in the main session stays there. To guarantee it has the conventions from the start, preload them: the `skills` field injects each listed skill's full content at startup. Choice D is the near miss, because the subagent **can** still invoke the skill itself through the Skill tool, but that happens only if it decides to, not at startup.

stem: Your Agent SDK agent runs long sessions. After automatic compaction it forgets a rule you gave only in the first prompt, and loses track of which files it had changed. Which changes address this?

choices.text: Lower `max_turns` so each run ends before compaction can trigger
choices.reason: `max_turns` caps tool-use round trips and ends the run with `error_max_turns`; it cuts the work short rather than keeping early context.

choices.text: Move the persistent rule out of the first prompt and into CLAUDE.md
choices.reason: Correct: compaction may not preserve instructions from early in the conversation, while CLAUDE.md content is re-injected on every request.

choices.text: Add a `PreCompact` hook that archives the full transcript to disk
choices.reason: Archiving keeps a copy for **you**; hooks run in your application, not in Claude's context, so Claude still works from the summary.

choices.text: Send `/compact` as a prompt more often so that each summary stays shorter
choices.reason: Manual compaction is still compaction: it also replaces older messages with a summary, so early details can still be lost.

choices.text: Add a CLAUDE.md section telling the compactor to keep modified file paths
choices.reason: Correct: the compactor reads CLAUDE.md, so a section saying what to preserve, such as file paths read or modified, shapes the summary.

takeaway: Summarized memory can drop early details: keep **standing rules in CLAUDE.md** and tell the compactor what to preserve.
explanation: Compaction replaces older messages with a summary, so a rule that lives only in the first prompt is at risk. CLAUDE.md fixes both symptoms: it's re-injected on every request, and the compactor reads it for instructions on what to keep. Choice C is the tempting distractor, because a `PreCompact` hook does preserve the transcript, but only for your application, not for Claude.

stem: Your team plans to replace a fixed workflow with an autonomous agent so it can handle open-ended requests. A finance stakeholder asks what the switch usually costs. Per Anthropic's guidance on building effective agents, what's the honest answer?

choices.text: Nothing extra: agents skip needless steps, so they run faster and cheaper
choices.reason: The guidance says the opposite: agentic systems often trade latency and cost for better performance, and autonomy means higher costs.

choices.text: Flexibility: agents give up the model-driven decisions that workflows allow
choices.reason: This reverses the roles. Workflows follow predefined paths; agents are the option when flexibility and model-driven decision-making are needed.

choices.text: Accuracy: open-ended tasks are always solved better by a fixed workflow
choices.reason: Workflows suit well-defined tasks. Open-ended problems with an unpredictable number of steps are where agents fit.

choices.text: Often more latency and cost, in exchange for better task performance
choices.reason: Correct: agentic systems often trade latency and cost for better task performance, so weigh when that tradeoff makes sense.

takeaway: Agents often buy better task performance with **more latency and cost**; decide whether the task needs it.
explanation: The principle is a tradeoff: agentic systems often trade latency and cost for better task performance, and their autonomy brings higher costs and the potential for compounding errors. The stakeholder asked about cost, so the answer names that price. Choice A is the tempting myth that agents are cheaper because they skip steps; the guidance says the opposite.

stem: You're moving a support assistant from your own Messages API loop, where you resend the whole history on every turn, to a Claude Managed Agents session. The user replies to the agent mid-task. How should your app pass that reply on?

choices.text: Resend the full conversation history along with the reply in each new event you send
choices.reason: Managed Agents is stateful by design: sessions store conversation history server-side, so you don't rebuild and resend it.

choices.text: Start a new session for each reply, passing a summary of the earlier turns
choices.reason: Sessions are long-running and resume cleanly after pauses; one session is meant to span many interactions.

choices.text: Send it as a new user event to the same session; history is kept server-side
choices.reason: Correct: you send user messages as events, and event history is persisted server-side and can be fetched in full.

choices.text: Write the reply into the agent's system prompt and update the agent definition
choices.reason: The agent definition (model, system prompt, tools, MCP servers, skills) is created once and reused across sessions, not edited per turn.

takeaway: Managed Agents sessions are **stateful**: send just the new user event; history lives server-side.
explanation: The wiring path decides who keeps state. On your own loop you hold the history; Managed Agents stores conversation history, sandbox state and outputs server-side, so a reply is just another user event on the same session. Choice A is tempting because it's the habit carried over from the raw loop, but the harness already has the history.

stem: Compliance needs every tool result your Agent SDK agent receives written to an audit log. In your old hand-written loop you logged each result before sending it back. Now the SDK runs the loop. Where does the logging go?

choices.text: In your loop code, between receiving each tool call and returning that call's result
choices.reason: The SDK executes tools and feeds results back to Claude without yielding control to your code, so there's no such spot in your code.

choices.text: In a `PostToolUse` hook, which fires after each tool returns in your process
choices.reason: Correct: `PostToolUse` fires after a tool returns and is meant for auditing outputs. Hooks run in your application process, not in context.

choices.text: In the system prompt, asking Claude to repeat each tool result in its reply
choices.reason: That puts the record in Claude's hands and costs context. Hooks run in your app process and don't consume context.

choices.text: In a `PreCompact` hook, which receives each tool result before it's stored
choices.reason: `PreCompact` runs before context compaction, for example to archive the transcript. It doesn't fire for each tool call.

takeaway: When the SDK runs the loop, intercept tool calls with **hooks**: `PostToolUse` to audit outputs.
explanation: Handling the tool-use loop moves to the SDK: it runs each tool and feeds the result back without returning control to your code. So per-call logic goes in hooks, and `PostToolUse` fires after each tool returns, which is the audit point. Choice A is the tempting carry-over from a raw loop, but that code no longer exists.

stem: Your production Agent SDK agent takes open-ended prompts like "improve this codebase", and some runs go on far longer and cost far more than expected. Which options set a limit that ends a run?

choices.text: Set `max_turns` to cap how many tool-use round trips a run can take
choices.reason: Correct: `max_turns` caps tool-use round trips. It defaults to no limit, so without it the loop runs until Claude finishes.

choices.text: Set `effort` to `"low"` so each response uses fewer reasoning tokens
choices.reason: `effort` trades reasoning depth for cost within each response. It lowers per-turn spend but doesn't stop the loop.

choices.text: Add a `PreCompact` hook so the run ends when its context fills up
choices.reason: `PreCompact` runs custom logic before compaction, such as archiving the transcript. It doesn't end the run.

choices.text: Set `max_budget_usd` to stop the loop once estimated spend reaches a cap
choices.reason: Correct: the budget cap stops the loop at a spend threshold (it also defaults to no limit). A budget is a good default for production agents.

choices.text: Add a `Stop` hook so the agent can't keep calling tools past a set time
choices.reason: A `Stop` hook fires when the agent finishes, for checking the result or saving state; it doesn't cut a run short.

takeaway: Bound SDK runs with `max_turns` and `max_budget_usd`; both default to **no limit**.
explanation: Without limits the loop runs until Claude finishes on its own, which can run long on open-ended prompts. The two documented caps are `max_turns` (tool-use round trips) and `max_budget_usd` (estimated spend), and hitting either ends the run with an error subtype. Choice B is tempting because lower effort cuts cost, but it only trims each response.

stem: Your Agent SDK app must log every `Bash` command before it runs, including commands auto-approved through `allowed_tools`. Where should the logging go?

choices.text: In the system prompt, asking Claude to announce each command first
choices.reason: An instruction depends on Claude choosing to follow it; it isn't a check that runs in your code.

choices.text: In a `Stop` hook, which runs when the agent finishes
choices.reason: That runs after the commands have already executed, not before each one.

choices.text: In a `PreToolUse` hook, which runs before every tool call
choices.reason: Correct: a `PreToolUse` hook executes before the rest of the permission flow, for every call, auto-approved ones included.

choices.text: In the `canUseTool` callback, which runs for every tool call
choices.reason: The callback never fires for auto-approved tools, such as those listed in `allowed_tools`.

takeaway: `canUseTool` sees only calls nothing approved first; for **every** call, use a `PreToolUse` hook.
explanation: Tools listed in `allowed_tools` are auto-approved, and the docs note that the `canUseTool` callback never fires for auto-approved tools, so D misses them. Logic that must apply to every tool call belongs in a `PreToolUse` hook, which runs before the rest of the permission flow (C). A depends on Claude choosing to comply, and B runs only after the commands have executed.

stem: Your agent works through a long list of vendor contracts, drafting amendments with tools. Some contracts are missing data the agent can't resolve, and legal wants to review drafts at set points before anything is sent. Per Anthropic's Building effective agents post, how should the agent handle these moments?

choices.text: Pause for human feedback at those checkpoints or when it hits a blocker
choices.reason: Correct: agents can pause for human feedback at checkpoints or when encountering blockers.

choices.text: Keep working without people, since an agent that stops to ask isn't autonomous
choices.reason: The post describes pausing for human feedback at checkpoints or on blockers as part of how agents operate.

choices.text: Remove its stopping conditions so it can get through every contract unaided
choices.reason: The post says it's common to include stopping conditions, such as a maximum number of iterations, to maintain control.

choices.text: Fill in the missing data with its best guess so the run never has to stop
choices.reason: Agents need "ground truth" from the environment at each step to assess progress; a guess gives it none.

takeaway: Design agents to **pause for human feedback** at checkpoints and on blockers, and keep stopping conditions for control.
explanation: Autonomy doesn't mean no people: the post describes agents that work independently but pause for human feedback at checkpoints or when they hit a blocker. Here the missing data is a blocker and legal review is a checkpoint, so both are natural pauses. B is the tempting choice because it sounds like "more autonomous", but it removes the oversight the scenario requires.

stem: Your main SDK agent reviews pull requests. You split style, security and test-coverage checks into three subagents. Which benefits does that delegation actually give you?

choices.text: Each subagent inherits the main conversation, so its prompt can stay short
choices.reason: A non-fork subagent starts fresh with no parent conversation; the only content passed in is the Agent tool's prompt string.

choices.text: Each subagent's tool calls stay inside it; only its final message returns
choices.reason: Correct: context isolation. Intermediate tool calls and results stay in the subagent, so the parent gets a concise summary.

choices.text: Subagent spend falls outside `max_budget_usd`, so the cap counts less of it
choices.reason: The spend cap counts the query's own spend, subagent requests included.

choices.text: All subagents share the main context window, so tokens are only paid once
choices.reason: Each subagent runs in its own conversation and makes its own API requests, which count toward the total cost.

choices.text: Independent checks can run at the same time, so they finish sooner overall
choices.reason: Correct: parallelization. Independent subtasks finish in the time of the slowest one rather than the sum of all of them.

takeaway: Subagents buy **context isolation** and **parallelism**, not free tokens or shared history.
explanation: Each subagent runs in its own conversation and returns only its final message, which keeps the parent's context small, and independent subagents can run at the same time. They don't see the parent's history, and their spend counts toward the budget cap. Choice A is the most tempting mistake: a non-fork subagent sees only the prompt string it's given.

stem: Each morning a developer opens a new Claude Code session and has to tell Claude again: "run tests with `make test`, not `pytest`". Yesterday's correction is gone every time. What does the Claude Code memory documentation recommend?

choices.text: Add the rule to the project CLAUDE.md, which Claude reads at each session start
choices.reason: Correct: CLAUDE.md is for facts Claude should hold in every session, and typing the same correction you typed last session is a signal to add one.

choices.text: Repeat it once with more emphasis, so Claude carries the rule into the next session
choices.reason: Each Claude Code session begins with a fresh context window; chat from one session doesn't carry into the next.

choices.text: Run `/compact` before closing, so the summary carries into tomorrow's session
choices.reason: Compaction summarizes the current session. Knowledge crosses sessions through CLAUDE.md files and auto memory.

choices.text: Write a skill holding the rule, so its body loads into every session
choices.reason: A skill's body loads only when it's used. A one-line "always do X" fact belongs in CLAUDE.md; skills are for multi-step procedures.

takeaway: Typing the same correction every session? Put it in **CLAUDE.md**, which loads at every session start.
explanation: Each Claude Code session begins with a fresh context window, so a correction given only in chat disappears. CLAUDE.md is read at the start of every session, and the docs list "you type the same correction you typed last session" as a reason to add to it. Choice D is tempting, but a skill's body loads only on use and suits procedures, not one-line facts.

stem: In one Agent SDK session, turn 2 reads a 40,000-token log file. By turn 12, context use is far higher than your team estimated, because a teammate assumed each turn starts with a clean window. What's actually happening?

choices.text: The SDK re-reads the log file from disk on every turn to keep it current
choices.reason: Nothing re-reads the file. The output from turn 2 is simply still part of the conversation history.

choices.text: Only CLAUDE.md accumulates; tool outputs are dropped once a turn completes
choices.reason: CLAUDE.md is in every request, but tool inputs and outputs accumulate in the history too, turn after turn.

choices.text: Turns reset the window, but compaction adds older tool output back in later
choices.reason: Compaction replaces older history with a summary; it doesn't re-add old output. And turns don't reset the window.

choices.text: The window doesn't reset between turns, so the log stays in the history
choices.reason: Correct: within a session everything accumulates (prompt, tools, history, tool inputs and outputs), and large outputs use significant context.

takeaway: Within an SDK session, **tool outputs stay in context** and accumulate turn after turn.
explanation: In-context memory grows with every turn: the context window doesn't reset between turns within a session, so the big log read in turn 2 is still there in turn 12. Large tool outputs are a main reason long sessions build up context. Choice B is tempting because CLAUDE.md is the thing people know is "always loaded", but tool output accumulates too.

stem: You're adding Claude's memory tool to your Messages API agent so it can keep notes across conversations. A teammate assumes Anthropic will store the memory files and plans no storage of your own. What does the memory tool actually require from your app?

choices.text: Only the `tools` entry: Anthropic stores each key's `/memories` files
choices.reason: The memory tool is client-side: memory lives entirely in your application, not on Anthropic's side.

choices.text: A handler that runs each memory command on storage you control
choices.reason: Correct: Claude only requests memory operations; your application executes them on storage you control and returns a `tool_result`.

choices.text: A custom `input_schema` that describes each memory command
choices.reason: The `tools` entry is the entire configuration; you don't define an input schema for an Anthropic-provided tool.

choices.text: A system-prompt section telling Claude to view its memory first
choices.reason: When the memory tool is in `tools`, the API adds that memory protocol to the system prompt automatically.

takeaway: The memory tool is **client-side**: Claude requests file operations, and your handler executes them on storage you control.
explanation: The memory tool follows the client-tool contract: Claude emits a `tool_use` for a command such as `view` or `create`, and **your application** executes it against storage you control, such as a per-user directory (B). A is the assumption in the stem: nothing is stored on Anthropic's side. C adds a schema the Anthropic-provided tool doesn't take, and D repeats an instruction the API already adds.

stem: Your long-running agent uses compaction to keep its context small. After older turns are summarized, it loses track of key decisions it made hours earlier. What does the memory tool documentation suggest?

choices.text: Turn compaction off and keep every turn of the conversation in context
choices.reason: Compaction exists because long conversations approach the context window limit; turning it off doesn't solve that.

choices.text: Pair compaction with the memory tool, so must-keep facts live outside context
choices.reason: Correct: for long-running agents, compaction keeps the active context small and memory preserves what must survive summarization.

choices.text: Have Anthropic keep the agent's memory files on its servers between sessions
choices.reason: The memory tool is client-side: Claude requests file operations and your application stores the data.

choices.text: Swap compaction for context editing, which summarizes the conversation on the server
choices.reason: Context editing clears specific tool results on the client; compaction is the server-side summary.

takeaway: Use **compaction and memory together**: compaction keeps context small, memory keeps what summaries might lose.
explanation: Compaction replaces older turns with a summary, so details can drop out. The memory tool stores information in files outside the context window, which a summary can't erase, and the docs suggest using both for long-running agents. D is tempting because context editing also manages context, but it clears specific tool results on the client rather than summarizing.

stem: You're choosing long-horizon context techniques for several agents. Anthropic's context engineering post says the choice depends on task characteristics. Which pairings match its guidance?

choices.text: Iterative development with clear milestones → compaction
choices.reason: The post pairs iterative development with clear milestones with structured note-taking, not compaction.

choices.text: Extensive back-and-forth conversation → multi-agent subagents
choices.reason: The post matches multi-agent architectures to complex research and analysis, not to conversational back-and-forth.

choices.text: Extensive back-and-forth conversation → compaction
choices.reason: Correct: compaction suits tasks requiring extensive back-and-forth, because it keeps the conversation flowing.

choices.text: Milestone-driven development → subagents returning short summaries
choices.reason: Milestone-driven work is matched to structured note-taking, where notes persist outside the context window.

choices.text: Complex parallel research and analysis → multi-agent architecture
choices.reason: Correct: multi-agent architectures handle complex research and analysis where parallel exploration pays dividends.

takeaway: Back-and-forth → **compaction**; milestones → **note-taking**; parallel research → **multi-agent**.
explanation: The post ties each technique to a kind of task: compaction for extensive back-and-forth, structured note-taking for iterative development with clear milestones, and multi-agent architectures for complex research where parallel exploration pays off. Choice A is the tempting swap, because milestone work also runs long, but its match is note-taking.

stem: Your multi-tenant support app uses the memory tool. Your handler maps `/memories` to one shared directory for every customer, and Claude starts quoting one customer's notes to another. What's the right fix?

choices.text: Give each customer its own tool name, such as `memory_acme`, in `tools`
choices.reason: The tool's `name` must be `memory`. Separation comes from what storage your handler serves, not the tool name.

choices.text: Tell Claude in the system prompt to ignore files about other customers
choices.reason: That leaves every customer's files in reach. Memory lives entirely in your application, so isolation belongs in the handler.

choices.text: Ask Anthropic to partition the memory store separately for each API key
choices.reason: Anthropic doesn't hold the files. The tool is client-side, and your application executes every operation.

choices.text: Map the `/memories` prefix to per-customer storage, like one directory each
choices.reason: Correct: `/memories` is a prefix your handler maps onto real storage, such as a per-user directory or keys in a database.

takeaway: Your handler decides what `/memories` means; map it to **per-user storage** to keep memories apart.
explanation: With the memory tool, Claude only requests operations; your handler decides which real storage `/memories` refers to. A later conversation sees whatever store your handler serves, so a single shared directory mixes customers. Choice B is tempting because prompts steer behaviour, but the files would still be served to every customer's conversation.

diagram.caption: Claude asks; your handler picks the store.

stem: Your Agent SDK agent can run `Bash`. Its system prompt says "Never run destructive commands such as `rm -rf`." In testing it still ran one once. You need destructive commands blocked every time, before they execute. What should you add?

choices.text: The same rule in capitals at both the start and end of the prompt
choices.reason: Any prompt wording is still a request to the model; a `PreToolUse` hook runs your own code before each tool call.

choices.text: A `PreToolUse` hook on `Bash` that returns a `deny` decision
choices.reason: Correct: `PreToolUse` fires before the call runs, and returning `permissionDecision: "deny"` blocks the operation.

choices.text: A `PostToolUse` hook that inspects each command after it runs
choices.reason: `PostToolUse` fires after the tool returns its result, so the destructive command would already have run.

choices.text: A `Stop` hook that reviews the session's commands at the end
choices.reason: `Stop` fires when execution stops, far too late to prevent a command that already ran.

takeaway: To enforce a rule every time, use a **`PreToolUse` hook** that denies the call: your code runs on each call, while a prompt rule is only a request.
explanation: Hooks are your own code running at fixed points in the loop, so they can **block dangerous operations before they execute**. A `PreToolUse` hook matched to `Bash` sees each command and can return a `deny` decision (B). A is the tempting trap: stronger wording still leaves the choice to the model, which already broke the rule once. C and D fire only after the command has run.

source.title: Intercept and control agent behavior with hooks

stem: Two teams are choosing how to run their agents. Team 1 needs a nightly agent that runs for hours with shell access in a sandbox, and wants no agent loop or sandbox to build or operate. Team 2 needs fine-grained control over every step of a custom loop. Which split fits Anthropic's guidance?

choices.text: Team 1 on the Messages API, Team 2 on Claude Managed Agents
choices.reason: Reversed: Managed Agents is best for long-running, asynchronous work; the Messages API suits custom loops and fine-grained control.

choices.text: Both on Claude Managed Agents, since it supports any custom loop
choices.reason: Managed Agents is a pre-built harness; custom agent loops with fine-grained control are what the Messages API is for.

choices.text: Team 1 on Claude Managed Agents, Team 2 on the Messages API
choices.reason: Correct: Managed Agents fits long-running tasks with minimal infrastructure; the Messages API fits custom loops and fine-grained control.

choices.text: Both on the Messages API, since Managed Agents can't run shell commands
choices.reason: Managed Agents includes built-in tools such as Bash, which runs shell commands in the sandbox.

takeaway: **Managed Agents** for long-running work without your own loop or sandbox; the **Messages API** for custom loops with fine-grained control.
explanation: Anthropic frames the choice by workload. Claude Managed Agents is a pre-built harness in managed infrastructure, best for **long-running, asynchronous** tasks with minimal infrastructure, which is Team 1. The Messages API gives direct model access, best for **custom agent loops and fine-grained control**, which is Team 2 (C). A is the tempting trap with the two swapped. B and D misstate what each option can do.

stem: Your research agent runs dozens of searches per question, and the raw results soon crowd its context window, so its final synthesis gets worse. Per Anthropic's context engineering post, which structure helps most?

choices.text: Keep every raw result in the lead agent's context so nothing is lost
choices.reason: That is the problem in the stem: raw search results bloat the lead agent's context window.

choices.text: Run all searches in the lead agent, restating the question after each
choices.reason: Restating adds tokens; it doesn't keep detailed search context out of the lead agent's window.

choices.text: Merge the searches into one broad query so fewer results come back
choices.reason: The post's remedy isn't fewer searches; it's isolating their detail in sub-agents with clean context windows.

choices.text: Have sub-agents search in clean contexts and return short summaries to a lead
choices.reason: Correct: each sub-agent may explore widely but returns a condensed summary (often 1,000–2,000 tokens) to the lead agent.

takeaway: Isolate heavy exploration in **sub-agents** with clean context windows; the lead agent receives only condensed summaries.
explanation: Sub-agent architectures give each focused task a clean context window: a sub-agent may explore extensively but returns only a **condensed summary**, often 1,000–2,000 tokens (D). That keeps detailed search context separate from the lead agent's synthesis. A is the current setup the stem describes. B and C keep all the raw detail in one window, which is what degrades the synthesis.

stem: Your coding agent works on a migration that spans many context windows. After each reset it redoes steps it already finished, because nothing tells it what's done. Which technique from Anthropic's context engineering post fits best?

choices.text: Raise `max_tokens` so each reply can restate all completed steps
choices.reason: Longer replies still live in the context window; notes kept outside the window are what survive a reset.

choices.text: Have the agent keep a progress file, like NOTES.md, outside its context
choices.reason: Correct: structured note-taking saves notes outside the context window and reloads them later, like an agent's NOTES.md file.

choices.text: Preload the whole repository into context at the start of each window
choices.reason: The post favors just-in-time retrieval: keep lightweight identifiers such as file paths and load data with tools when needed.

choices.text: Clear old tool results so each window can hold more of the history
choices.reason: Tool result clearing is a light form of compaction; it frees space but doesn't record which steps are done.

takeaway: For work that spans context resets, have the agent keep **structured notes** outside the window and reread them.
explanation: Structured note-taking means the agent writes notes **outside the context window**, such as a to-do list or a NOTES.md file, and reloads them later, so progress survives a reset (B). The stem's problem is lost progress, not lack of space. D is the tempting trap: clearing tool results frees room but records nothing. A keeps everything inside the window, and C floods it with data.

stem: Your team plans to replace a working single-agent research flow with a lead agent that fans out to parallel subagents and then synthesizes what they find. Which two costs should the team plan for?

choices.text: Each subagent shares the lead agent's context window, so the lead's context fills up much faster
choices.reason: Subagents operate in parallel with their own context windows; that separation is what lets them condense their findings for the lead.

choices.text: Much higher token use than a single agent, so the task's value has to justify the spend
choices.reason: Correct: multi-agent systems used about 15× more tokens than chats (single agents about 4×), so they need tasks valuable enough to pay for it.

choices.text: Harder coordination between agents, and errors that compound because agents carry state across steps
choices.reason: Correct: the post says agents are stateful and errors compound, so minor issues can derail them, and agents aren't yet great at coordinating in real time.

choices.text: A guaranteed slowdown, because parallel subagents always take longer than one agent working serially
choices.reason: Running subagents in parallel cut research time by up to 90% for complex queries in Anthropic's system.

choices.text: Subagents can't call tools, so all of the searching must still be done by the lead agent itself
choices.reason: In Anthropic's system, subagents iteratively use search tools themselves and return their findings to the lead.

takeaway: Orchestrator-worker buys breadth with **tokens** and **coordination risk**; it's worth it only for valuable, truly parallel tasks.
explanation: A planning, fan-out and synthesis structure is a deliberate trade-off: parallel subagents bring breadth and speed but multiply token use and add coordination and compounding-error risk. The stem's team already has a working single agent, so these costs decide whether the switch pays off. Choice d is tempting because more agents sounds slower, but parallel subagents actually cut research time.

source.title: How we built our multi-agent research system

stem: Your coding agent's tasks are tightly linked: each change depends on decisions made in the previous one, and every step needs the full picture of the codebase. A teammate proposes fanning out to parallel subagents to finish faster. What does Anthropic's multi-agent post suggest?

choices.text: A strong fit, since any task gets faster when more agents work on it at the same time
choices.reason: The post says some domains aren't a good fit today, such as those that need one shared context or have many dependencies between agents.

choices.text: A strong fit, as long as every subagent receives a full copy of the lead agent's context window
choices.reason: Subagents work with their own context windows, and the post notes that most coding tasks involve fewer truly parallelizable tasks than research.

choices.text: A weak fit only because subagents cost more tokens; once tokens are cheaper it becomes ideal
choices.reason: Token cost matters, but the post's concern here is structural: shared context, dependencies between agents, and agents that still coordinate poorly in real time.

choices.text: A weak fit: work that needs one shared context or has many dependencies doesn't suit multi-agent yet
choices.reason: Correct: domains that require all agents to share the same context or involve many dependencies between agents aren't a good fit for multi-agent systems today.

takeaway: Fan out only when the work **splits into independent parts**; dependent steps with shared context belong in one agent.
explanation: Parallel subagents help when a task splits into independent parts that can run separately. The stem's work is the opposite: each step depends on the last and needs the same full context, which the post names as a poor fit. Choice c is tempting because cost is a real downside, but the deciding problem here is the dependencies, not the price.

stem: Your research agent gives good answers but is slow: it runs one search, reads the results, then runs the next search, one after another. The searches don't depend on each other. Which change cuts the wait?

choices.text: Run several subagents in parallel, and let each one call several tools in parallel too
choices.reason: Correct: the lead spins up 3–5 subagents in parallel rather than serially, and subagents use 3+ tools in parallel, which cut research time by up to 90% for complex queries.

choices.text: Cap each run at a single search so that the agent stops reading results it might not need
choices.reason: The post's early agents were slow because they searched sequentially; the fix kept searching and made it parallel rather than cutting it.

choices.text: Put all the source material into one large prompt and let the model answer without any tools
choices.reason: The system is built on searching with tools; its speed-up came from parallel subagents and parallel tool calls, not from dropping tools.

choices.text: Make the agent finish each search and analyze it fully before it is allowed to start the next
choices.reason: That is the sequential pattern the post describes as painfully slow; the fix was parallelism at two levels.

takeaway: When the work is independent, **parallel subagents and parallel tool calls** cut wall-clock time, at the price of more tokens.
explanation: Sequential searching makes latency add up step by step, while independent searches can run at the same time. Anthropic parallelized at two levels, subagents and their tool calls, and research time dropped sharply on complex queries. Choice d is tempting because it sounds careful, but it is exactly the slow sequential pattern the stem describes.

stem: Your assistant answers research questions with one retrieval step: it fetches the chunks most similar to the question, then writes its answer. Questions where the first results reveal new leads get poor answers. What would agentic search change?

choices.text: It retrieves many more chunks in that single step, so that the new leads are already included
choices.reason: That is still static retrieval done once; the new leads only become visible after the first results have been read.

choices.text: The model searches step by step with tools, adapting each query to what it has found so far
choices.reason: Correct: Anthropic contrasts RAG's static retrieval with a multi-step search that dynamically finds relevant information and adapts to new findings.

choices.text: It embeds the documents with a stronger model, so that the one retrieval step is more accurate
choices.reason: Better embeddings still give one fixed retrieval pass; agentic search lets the model search again based on what it learned.

choices.text: It precomputes answers to likely questions ahead of time, so that no search is needed at all
choices.reason: The point is the opposite: searching at answer time, iteratively, so the model can follow leads that only appear in the results.

takeaway: **Agentic search**: the model searches iteratively with tools, refining its next query from what it found, instead of one static retrieval.
explanation: Static retrieval fetches similar chunks once, before the model has seen anything, so it can't follow up on what those chunks reveal. Agentic search puts the model in charge of a search loop, so each query can build on the last results. Choice a is tempting because more chunks sounds more thorough, but it's still a single pass that can't react to new leads.
